title: Workforce planning: Training and retention accompany displacement
desc: Describes automation, augmentation and redeployment together, emphasizing organizational barriers and incomplete worker transitions.

kps.k: The cluster frames workforce transformation as a skills and organisational challenge, not simply a technology-adoption problem.
kps.d: The Future of Jobs Report 2025 draws on 2024 employer expectations for 2025–2030. Skills gaps lead perceived transformation barriers at 63%, ranking first in 52 of 55 economies and 19 of 22 sectors. Employers also identify cultural resistance (46%), regulation (39%) and inadequate data and technical infrastructure (32%). The practical implication is that technology investment alone may not address the constraints employers anticipate; training, process redesign and organisational adaptation also feature.

kps.k: Employers plan automation alongside augmentation and redeployment, while still anticipating displacement.
kps.d: The report’s global benchmarks project predominantly human tasks falling from 48% to 33% by 2030, predominantly technology-delivered tasks rising from 22% to 34%, and combined work increasing from 30% to 33%. Employers plan upskilling (85%), automation (73%) and technological augmentation (63%). AI-specific plans include training existing workers to work alongside AI (77%), hiring AI-design capabilities (69%) and internal redeployment from AI-declining jobs (47%). Yet 41% foresee staff reductions due to skills obsolescence. This is a tension within employers’ plans, not evidence that augmentation or substitution will prevail; employer shares and task shares do not measure percentages of jobs lost.

kps.k: Training anchors the proposed response, but employers expect some workers to miss that transition.
kps.d: For a representative 100 workers, the report anticipates 29 receiving training within their current role, 19 receiving training and redeployment, 11 being unlikely to upskill, and 41 needing no training by 2030. Employers expect training to improve productivity (77%), competitiveness (70%) and retention (65%). These figures establish anticipated needs and business rationales, not measured returns or proof that training will prevent displacement. The practical challenge extends beyond offering courses to enabling role transitions and reaching workers unlikely to receive or complete upskilling.

kps.k: Talent strategies combine development with retention and wider recruitment, rather than relying exclusively on new technical hires.
kps.d: Employers identify employee well-being (64%) and effective reskilling and upskilling (63%) as promising ways to improve talent availability. Their strategies also include promotion pathways, higher wages, remote work and broader talent pools. Public-policy preferences favour training funding (55%), training provision (52%) and education improvements (47%). Priorities vary: 71% of Slovenian respondents favour hiring-and-firing flexibility, while South African respondents emphasise training funding and education improvements, both at 63%. These are employer preferences and plans, not demonstrated policy effects.

kps.k: Sector variation and the survey’s scope limit conclusions about AI’s effects on legal employment.
kps.d: Professional services reports 95% of organisations running AI programmes, 41% expected core-skill disruption and 19% five-year structural labour-force churn. These measures neither isolate law firms nor establish AI-caused job losses. Differences elsewhere also qualify global averages: healthcare employers cite cultural resistance more often than skills gaps, while energy technology and utilities employers report particularly acute skills gaps. The report considers AI alongside economic, demographic, climate and geopolitical pressures. The supplied material presents no competing-source disagreement or causal test; it offers a differentiated map of employer expectations rather than evidence that particular workforce interventions succeed.

vlens.an: The supplied market-analysis source supports the proposition that workforce planning combines training, augmentation and redeployment with continuing displacement risk. The Future of Jobs Report 2025 presents employers as pursuing upskilling and technology-enabled augmentation alongside automation, while some also expect reductions caused by skills obsolescence. It likewise supports framing transformation as an organisational and skills challenge rather than a technology-only exercise, identifying skills gaps, cultural resistance, regulation and infrastructure as constraints. Material variation lies across sectors, regions and worker outcomes: priorities and expected disruption differ, and some workers are expected to be redeployed while others may not upskill. These are survey-based employer expectations and plans for 2025–2030, not observed employment effects, causal evidence that AI produces the projected changes, or proof that training will secure successful transitions. Because the evidence comes from one report in a curated corpus, it should not be treated as representative of all market analysts, consultancies or press sources.

elens.an: The 2025-period source supports the proposition that workforce planning combines training, retention and technological augmentation with automation and possible displacement. Its employer-survey evidence treats skills gaps, organisational resistance, regulation and infrastructure as constraints on transformation, so adoption at scale is not framed as technology deployment alone. It also records plans to upskill, augment and redeploy workers while some employers anticipate staff reductions from skills obsolescence. Material variation appears across sectors and regions in the severity of skills disruption, leading barriers and preferred talent policies. The evidence remains prospective: it reports selected employers’ expectations and intentions for 2025–2030, not realised workforce effects, successful transitions or AI-caused legal-sector job losses.
